evidence: Hor. S. 1.1.96: ita sordidus, ut sē nōn umquam servō melius vestīret (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: First “dirty”, then “mean, niggardly” (Lewis & Short), of the miser in Horace who dressed no better than his slave.

evidence: Prop. 3.17.18: astrictus pater (Lewis & Short s.v. astringō)
terms.comment: Literally “drawn tight”: the participle of adstringō (also spelled astringō) used as an adjective of a person close with money. Lewis & Short: “sparing, parsimonious”, not before the Augustan period.

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
